title: Thousands of GPU servers exposed online, risking AI workloads
key_facts: Researchers at datacenter-security startup Lava found about 2,100 GPU servers exposing Nvidia DCGM Exporter monitoring data to the open internet, with no authentication.
Four scans between March and May 2026 found more than 12,000 GPUs, worth about $100 million, at nearly 300 organisations; 44% were in the US.
A flaw tracked as CVE-2026-47483, rated 8.2 (high), could let an unauthenticated attacker crash the monitoring service and disrupt AI workloads.
Hundreds of the exposed exporters were potentially vulnerable.
Nvidia fixed it in version 4.8.2; operators should upgrade and keep monitoring tools off the public internet.
Exposed hosts belonged to customers of GPU cloud providers including Voltage Park, Lambda, Northern Data and DigitalOcean; Lava told the providers.
Lava also found 12,096 public Node Exporter hosts leaking server and network details.
quote_evidence: Over the course of four scans between March and May, the threat hunters found about 2,100 GPU servers exposing DCGM Exporter metrics to the open internet.

These GPUs represented about $100 million in hardware, and included Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs, H200s, and H100s - used to run large-scale AI workloads - plus consumer RTX 5090 and 4090 systems.
Nvidia fixed the issue in version 4.8.2, and operators should upgrade to that version or later.
why_it_matters_hint: Misconfigured monitoring tools on costly AI servers reveal how they are built and can be crashed.
event_date: Lava blog Thursday 8 Oct 2026; scans March to May 2026
notes: SC Media page blocked (403). Read The Register and Help Net Security, which agree on the findings. Patch timing differs: Register says Nvidia fixed it in September, Help Net says the bulletin was 28 July 2026; the entry gives no date. Research is from 8 Oct, flaw itself older.
